extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (and patent practitioners) evaluating §101 patent-eligibility
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for performing the Alice/Mayo two-part test under 35 U.S.C. §101, including Step 2A Prong Two (particular treatment/prophylaxis integration) and Step 2B (search for an inventive concept). Aimed at evaluating whether claims are directed to judicial exceptions and whether additional elements provide 'significantly more.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Particular treatment and prophylaxis consideration (Step 2A Prong Two)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim reciting a judicial exception is not directed to the judicial exception if it also recites additional element(s) demonstrating that the claim as a whole integrates the exception into a practical application; one way to demonstrate such integration is when the additional elements apply or use the recited judicial exception to effect a particular treatment or prophylaxis for a disease or medical condition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanation and examples (Vanda Pharm. v. West-Ward): using a law of nature to effect a safer treatment (e.g., genotyping assay + dose adjustment) can render claims not 'directed to' the judicial exception at Step 2A. Examples of treatments/prophylaxis include acupuncture, administration of medication, dialysis, organ transplants, phototherapy, physiotherapy, radiation therapy, surgery, immunization steps that lower risk of later disease (Classen).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim limitation must affirmatively recite an action that effects treatment or prophylaxis
rubrics_metrics.description: To qualify as a 'treatment' or 'prophylaxis' limitation, the claim limitation must affirmatively recite an action that effects a particular treatment or prophylaxis for a disease or medical condition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positive examples: 'administering amazonic acid to a patient', 'administering a course of plasmapheresis to a patient.' Non-examples: intended use or field-of-use language (e.g., 'prescribing a topical steroid to a patient with eczema' is not positive because it does not require actual use), mere recitations that a product is a 'pharmaceutical composition' or that a device 'is operable to dispense' are not affirmative treatment limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Particularity or Generality of the Treatment or Prophylaxis
rubrics_metrics.description: The treatment or prophylaxis limitation must be 'particular,' i.e., specifically identified so that it does not encompass all applications of the judicial exception(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Particular example: 'administering a lower than normal dosage of a beta blocker medication to a patient identified as having the poor metabolizer genotype' integrates the abstract mental analysis into a practical application. Generic example: 'administering a suitable medication to a patient' is not particular and merely applies the exception generically. Examiners may consider related considerations such as mere instructions to apply an exception and field-of-use/technological environment when assessing particularity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether the limitation(s) have more than a nominal or insignificant relationship to the exception(s)
rubrics_metrics.description: The treatment/prophylaxis limitation must have more than a nominal or insignificant relationship to the recited judicial exception(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example where relationship is significant: reciting 'treating a patient having blood glucose >250 mg/dl with insulin' — insulin reduces glucose and reduces ketoacidosis risk, so it integrates the natural correlation into a practical application. Example where relationship is nominal: 'treating a patient having blood glucose >250 mg/dl with aspirin' — aspirin is not a treatment for ketoacidosis and thus has at best a nominal connection. Examiners may consider insignificant extra-solution activity and field-of-use considerations when evaluating significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitation must not be merely extra-solution activity or a field-of-use
rubrics_metrics.description: The treatment or prophylaxis limitation must impose meaningful limits on the judicial exception and cannot be merely extra-solution activity or a field-of-use limitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example of extra-solution activity: administering vaccines to gather data for later mental analysis (data-gathering as precursor) — this is not integration. Contrasting example: using analysis results to vaccinate a second group according to a lowest-risk schedule — that applying step integrates the abstract idea into a practical application. Examiners should evaluate insignificant extra-solution activity and field-of-use/technological environment considerations when making this determination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive concept definition (Step 2B): additional elements must amount to 'significantly more'
rubrics_metrics.description: An 'inventive concept' is furnished by an element or combination of elements recited in the claim in addition to (beyond) the judicial exception, and is sufficient to ensure the claim as a whole amounts to significantly more than the judicial exception itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The inventive concept cannot be supplied by the unpatentable law of nature, natural phenomenon, or abstract idea itself. Evaluate whether additional elements, individually or in combination, provide significantly more than the judicial exception so that the claim amounts to eligible subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider additional elements both individually and in combination
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluating whether additional elements amount to an inventive concept requires considering them both individually and in combination to ensure they amount to significantly more than the judicial exception itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consideration in combination is important because individually conventional elements can amount to significantly more when non-conventionally arranged (e.g., BASCOM: remote installation of filtering tool with customizable features). Courts consider claim elements 'as a whole' (Diamond v. Diehr).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conventionality / routine character is relevant but distinct from novelty/obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Although courts evaluate conventionality of an additional element in eligibility analysis, the search for an inventive concept is not a novelty (§102) or obviousness (§103) determination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lack of novelty under §102 or obviousness under §103 is 'of no relevance' to the §101 question of whether a claim falls within patent-eligible categories. The inventive concept inquiry is distinct: an inventive concept can be found in a non-conventional and non-generic arrangement of known, conventional pieces (e.g., BASCOM, Rapid Litigation Mgmt. v. CellzDirect). Patentability under §§102/103 is neither required for nor dispositive of §101 eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvements to the functioning of a computer can supply an inventive concept
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitations that improve the functioning of a computer (e.g., modification of conventional Internet hyperlink protocol) have been found to qualify as 'significantly more.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: DDR Holdings — modification that dynamically produces a dual-source hybrid webpage was an improvement to computer functioning and considered a qualifying limitation. See MPEP § 2106.05(a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvements to any other technology or technical field can supply an inventive concept
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitations that improve another technology or technical field (e.g., adding a thermocouple in a rubber-molding process to monitor temperature) can qualify as 'significantly more.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Diamond v. Diehr — modification to rubber curing process that reduced under- and over-curing. See MPEP § 2106.05(a)-(c).

rubrics_metrics.name: Applying the judicial exception with, or by use of, a particular machine
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying the judicial exception with or by use of a particular machine (with specific structure arranged to achieve a technical result) can supply an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: using a Fourdrinier machine arranged in a particular way to optimize speed while maintaining quality (Eibel Process). See MPEP § 2106.05(b).

rubrics_metrics.name: Effecting a transformation or reduction of a particular article to a different state or thing
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed process that effects a transformation or reduction of a particular article to a different state or thing can supply an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: transformation of raw, uncured synthetic rubber into precision-molded products (Diehr). See MPEP § 2106.05(c).

rubrics_metrics.name: Adding a specific limitation beyond well-understood, routine, conventional activity or adding unconventional steps that confine the claim
rubrics_metrics.description: Adding a specific limitation other than well-understood, routine, conventional activity in the field, or adding unconventional steps that confine the claim to a particular useful application, may supply an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: non-conventional and non-generic arrangement of computer components for filtering Internet content (BASCOM) — the arrangement, though consisting of known components, was non-conventional and provided significantly more. See MPEP § 2106.05(d).

rubrics_metrics.name: Other meaningful limitations beyond generally linking the exception to a technological environment
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitations providing meaningful constraints beyond merely linking the judicial exception to a particular technological environment can supply an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: an immunization step that integrates data comparison into a specific process of immunizing that lowers the risk of later disease (Classen). Such meaningful limitations go beyond merely stating a technological environment. See MPEP § 2106.05(e).

rubrics_metrics.name: Adding 'apply it' or mere instructions to implement an abstract idea on a computer is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Adding the words 'apply it' (or equivalent), or mere instructions to implement an abstract idea on a computer, does not amount to significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: indicating that a function like creating and maintaining electronic records is performed by a computer is insufficient (Alice). See MPEP § 2106.05(f).

rubrics_metrics.name: Simply appending well-understood, routine, conventional activities at a high level is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Appending well-understood, routine, conventional activities previously known to the industry, specified at a high level of generality, does not supply an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: claims that require no more than a generic computer to perform generic computer functions are insufficient (Alice). See MPEP § 2106.05(d).

rubrics_metrics.name: Adding insignificant extra-solution activity is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Adding insignificant extra-solution activity (e.g., mere data gathering) to the judicial exception does not amount to significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: obtaining information about transactions so the information can be analyzed by an abstract mental process (CyberSource). See MPEP § 2106.05(g).

rubrics_metrics.name: Generally linking the use of the judicial exception to a particular technological environment or field of use is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Generally linking an abstract idea or other judicial exception to a particular technological environment or field of use does not provide significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: limiting a hedging abstract idea to commodities markets (Bilski) or limiting a mathematical formula to petrochemical fields (Parker v. Flook). See MPEP § 2106.05(h).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere physicality/tangibility of additional elements is not a relevant consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: Mere physical or tangible implementation of an exception (e.g., invoking a computer because it is tangible) is not in itself an inventive concept and does not guarantee eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The fact that a computer is a tangible system is 'beside the point' (Alice). Conversely, the presence of a non-physical or intangible additional element does not doom eligibility — improvements need not be defined by physical components (Enfish, McRO). Examiners should not treat tangibility alone as dispositive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use judicial decisions as analytic examples when conducting the 'significantly more' analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: When conducting the Step 2B significantly more analysis, courts' approaches (e.g., Alice, BASCOM, DDR, Diehr, Vanda, Mayo) provide models for: identifying additional elements, considering elements individually, and considering them as an ordered combination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alice: identified additional elements (computer functions/hardware), found them well-understood/routine and the combination added nothing significantly more. BASCOM: emphasized evaluating arrangement in combination, where non-conventional arrangement of known elements supplied an inventive concept. Use these case analyses to guide claim parsing and weighing of elements.
